subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
passage: "Where were you?" Danish's mother, Preeti, asked as the door opened. "At the park," said Danish. "With Sohail. We played cricket." "The park is fine. Which way did you come back?" Danish looked at his shoes. "The usual way." "The usual way, or through the market road?" No answer. "Danish. I told you the market road has trucks." "I told you the truth! I was at the park." Preeti sat down slowly. "You told me the truth about the park and left out the part that matters. That is still hiding something." Danish's ears turned pink. "Next time tell me the whole thing," she said, "and we will find a safe way to go together."

qa.q: Which road had Preeti told Danish to avoid?
qa.a: She had told him to avoid the market road.

qa.q: What did Danish believe about what he told his mother?
qa.a: He believed it was fine because what he said about the park was true, though looking at his shoes suggests some unease about the road.

qa.q: What could Danish have said, and why would it help?
qa.a: He could have told the whole route, including the market road, and asked for a safe way, because his mother could then help with the risk.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about the half-truth?
qa.a: Worried about the trucks and hurt that the important part was left out, since she said it was still hiding something.

grounding: A boy tells only the park part of his outing and leaves out the road he was told to avoid, so the risk stays hidden from his mother.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
passage: Last summer Mummy asked where I'd been all afternoon, and I said, "At the park with Raghav." That was true. What I didn't say was how we got there. I'm Madhav. We'd taken the shortcut across the main road by the petrol pump, the one Mummy had told me three times never to cross alone. I told myself I hadn't lied. Every word was true. But that night I heard Mummy telling Papa, "At least he stays inside the colony, so I don't worry." And I realised my half-truth wasn't small at all. She felt safe because I'd hidden the dangerous part. I lay awake for a long time. Next morning I told her about the road.

qa.q: Where had Madhav said he'd been?
How did Madhav feel after hearing Mummy talk to Papa?
qa.a: Guilty and uneasy, lying awake for a long time.

qa.q: What else could Madhav have done?
qa.a: Told the whole truth straight away, or asked Mummy to walk them the long way round.

qa.q: What would change for Mummy once she knows about the road?
qa.a: She can plan a safer route or go with them, instead of feeling safe for the wrong reason.

grounding: Looking back, a boy tells only part of the truth about where he went, hiding a risky road from his parents until he owns up.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
passage:
Day-care note, Monday.
Farhan came back from the playground twenty minutes late today. When I asked, he said, "I was at the playground, Usha-aunty." That was true; I had seen him there. But his shoes were covered in the grey mud found only on the canal path, the path all the children have been told not to use because the edge is broken. I asked him gently, "Which way did you come back?" He looked away and said, "The normal way," then, after a moment, "Mostly." He had not lied exactly, but he had left out the part that mattered. I sat with him and explained that the unsafe part is exactly what adults need to know. I have called his mother today, and tomorrow I will walk the children back myself.
Usha, day-care

qa.q: What might Farhan have felt when he said 'Mostly'?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty, knowing he had left out the canal path.

qa.q: What else could Farhan have said?
qa.a: The whole truth about the canal path, so the adults could keep him safe.

qa.q: How does Usha see Farhan's half-truth?
qa.a: Usha sees that it hid the one part that mattered, and takes protective steps the same day.

grounding: A carer's note records a boy who tells a true but partial account, hiding that he used a forbidden, unsafe path.
